title: Slicing Strings
intro: A **slice** takes a piece of a string: `text[start:stop]` gives the characters from `start` up to, but **not including**, `stop`. Leave out `start` to begin at the start, or `stop` to run to the end. A third number, `step`, skips characters.

questions.prompt: Slices never crash, even if the numbers run past the end. A step of `-1` walks backwards, which reverses the text.
questions.exampleCode:
code = "PY-2026-XL"
print(code[0:2])
print(code[3:7])
print(code[-2:])
print(code[::2])
print(code[::-1])
questions.explanation: `code[3:7]` is indexes 3, 4, 5 and 6 — four characters. `stop` is never included.

questions.prompt: `date_text` holds a date like `2026-10-29`. Slice it into `year` (first 4 characters), `month` (the 2 after the first dash) and `day` (the last 2).
questions.solution:
year = date_text[0:4]
month = date_text[5:7]
day = date_text[-2:]

tests.name: year
tests.code: assert year == date_text[:4], 'year should be the first 4 characters.'

tests.name: month
tests.code: assert month == date_text[5:7], 'month should be the 2 characters after the first dash (indexes 5 and 6).'

tests.name: day
tests.code: assert day == date_text[-2:], 'day should be the last 2 characters.'

questions.hint: Count the positions: the first dash is at index 4.
questions.explanation: Fixed-format text like dates and codes is a perfect fit for slicing.

questions.hint: Start at index 4 and run to the end.

questions.prompt: `word` holds a word. Store it reversed in `backwards`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert backwards == word[::-1], 'backwards should be word reversed.'
tests.message: backwards should be the word reversed.

questions.hint: A step of `-1` walks from the end to the start.
questions.explanation: `[::-1]` is the usual way to reverse a string in Python.

questions.prompt: `area_code` should be the first 3 digits of `phone` (`020`), but it comes out as `207`. Fix the slice.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert area_code == '020', 'area_code should be the first 3 characters: 020.'

questions.hint: The first character is at index 0.
questions.explanation: Off-by-one mistakes are common with slices. `phone[:3]` also works.

questions.prompt: The message is hidden in every other letter of `secret`. Fill in the slice so `message` is `python`.
questions.hint: Take every second character, starting from the first.

questions.prompt: `card` holds a card number as text. Store its last 4 digits in `last_four`, and in `masked` a string of `*` for every other digit followed by those 4 — so a 16-digit card becomes `************4444`.

tests.name: last
tests.code: assert last_four == card[-4:], 'last_four should be the last 4 characters.'

tests.name: masked
tests.code: assert masked == '*' * (len(card) - 4) + card[-4:], 'masked should hide every digit except the last 4 with *.'

tests.name: length
tests.code: assert len(masked) == len(card), 'masked should be as long as card.'
tests.message: masked should be as long as card.

questions.hint: How many stars? The length minus 4.
questions.explanation: Using `len(card)` makes it work for cards of any length.

questions.prompt: Slices don't crash when they run past the end. What does this print?
questions.hint: What's left when you start after the last character?
questions.explanation: The slice is simply empty — no *IndexError*, unlike `"abc"[5]`.

questions.prompt: A **palindrome** reads the same backwards, like `level`. Store in `is_palindrome` whether `word` is one — a single comparison is enough.

tests.name: bool
tests.code: assert isinstance(is_palindrome, bool), 'Store the comparison itself (True or False).'

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert is_palindrome == (word == word[::-1]), 'Compare word with itself reversed.'

questions.hint: Compare the word with its reverse using `==`.
questions.explanation: A slice plus a comparison answers the question in one line.
